stories.headline: Colorado sues Trump administration to block new ICE detention center in Hudson
stories.summary:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday seeking to block the Trump administration's plans to open a nearly 1,200-bed immigrant detention center in Hudson, roughly 30 miles northeast of Denver. The suit alleges that the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement violated environmental, immigration and procedural laws by contracting with the Geo Group to operate the facility — dubbed the Big Horn Facility — without conducting required reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act.

Weiser's office raised specific environmental concerns, including a deer corridor within a half-mile of the prison and a designated aquatic native species conservation area along nearby Box Elder Creek. The attorney general said construction and renovation of the long-shuttered private prison had already begun and asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction halting all work.

This is the third lawsuit filed in recent months attempting to block the facility. A Weld County resident and nonprofit group sued the town of Hudson in July, and GreenLatinos and the Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition filed a separate federal suit last week on similar NEPA grounds. The Department of Homeland Security said in an unsigned statement that the lawsuit was not about the environment but about stopping the administration's public safety agenda.

If the facility opens, it would nearly double Colorado's immigrant detention capacity. The state currently has one immigrant detention center, also operated by Geo Group, located in Aurora with a maximum capacity of 1,532 beds. The contract with Geo Group for the Hudson facility is valued at $528.6 million.

stories.headline: Ballot Issue 7A: Front Range voters to weigh sales tax hike for expanded passenger rail service
stories.summary:
Front Range voters in November will decide whether to approve a 0.333% sales tax increase — about 33 cents per $100 of taxable purchases — to fund expanded Colorado Connector passenger rail service stretching from Fort Collins to Pueblo. The measure, known as Ballot Issue 7A, would apply to approximately 2.4 million voters in roughly 30 communities across 13 counties that would be served by the rail line.

The Front Range Passenger Rail District says it already has $332 million secured to launch three daily round trips between Denver's Union Station and Fort Collins by 2029, using a state transportation innovation fund and RTD money set aside for unbuilt FasTracks lines. If 7A passes, the new sales tax would generate an estimated $295 million annually and allow the district to sell $580 million in bonds, funding full buildout to Colorado Springs and Pueblo at a total cost of $2.7 billion over five years.

Six Colorado professional sports franchises — the Broncos, Nuggets, Avalanche, Rockies, Summit FC and Colorado Mammoth — jointly endorsed the measure Tuesday, citing the planned special event stops near Ball Arena and the Broncos' planned Burnham Yard stadium site. Broncos president Damani Leech said the rail line would provide fans across the state with another convenient way to reach games.

The tax would not apply to items already exempt under state law, including most groceries, gas, prescription drugs, medical supplies and residential energy. The Front Range Passenger Rail District's board voted 14-1 in August to refer the measure to the ballot.

stories.headline: Colorado braces for most widespread rainfall in years as Hurricane Polo remnants approach
stories.summary:
The remnants of Hurricane Polo, currently spinning in the eastern Pacific Ocean near Mexico, are expected to merge with a storm system moving into the southwestern United States and produce Colorado's most widespread rainfall since May 2023, according to the National Weather Service. A moderate risk of flash flooding — at least 40% — is forecast for southern Colorado, while the Denver area and northeastern plains face a slight risk of at least 15%.

Flood watches are in effect from late Tuesday night through Thursday morning for much of Colorado's Front Range, Eastern Plains and southern regions, covering counties including Douglas, Jefferson, El Paso, Pueblo, Elbert and Lincoln, among others. The highest-risk areas include Pueblo, Walsenburg, Trinidad, Lamar and La Junta, where 2 to 5 inches of rain is expected. Denver is forecast to accumulate roughly 1.4 inches by Thursday morning, with communities near the Palmer Divide such as Parker and Castle Rock potentially seeing more than 2 inches.

NWS meteorologist Zach Hiris described Denver as 'firmly in the battleground,' caught between drier patterns to the north and tropical moisture hitting the south. Light to moderate rain is expected in the city, with flooding not currently a primary concern for Denver proper, though forecasters will monitor flood activity to the south.

Tuesday will bring cloudy skies and temperatures in the upper 60s along the I-25 corridor. The heaviest rain along the Front Range is expected Wednesday, with the storm system pushing out Thursday and clearing the way for sunshine and temperatures in the 70s by the weekend. Mountain snow could mix in at elevations above 11,000 feet if temperatures cool sufficiently.

stories.headline: Denver Water bans lawn watering starting Thursday, Oct. 1, citing severe drought
stories.summary:
The Denver Board of Water Commissioners announced that Denver Water will prohibit lawn watering beginning Thursday, Oct. 1, due to severe drought conditions. Violators face hefty fines under the Stage 1 drought resolution.

The ban arrives as a major rain event is forecast to move through Colorado midweek, though water officials said the short-term precipitation is not sufficient to lift the drought designation that triggered the mandatory restrictions. Customers are advised to check Denver Water's guidelines for what outdoor water uses remain permitted under Stage 1 restrictions.

The announcement adds a layer of complexity for Denver residents already dealing with an unusual weather pattern: a lawn-watering ban taking effect just as one of the wettest storms in years is expected to hit the region. Denver Water officials have not indicated when the ban might be lifted, which will depend on reservoir levels and ongoing drought assessments.

stories.headline: RTD A-Line to Denver airport cuts service in half through Oct. 10 for track repairs
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District's A-Line commuter rail service to Denver International Airport has been reduced to roughly half its normal frequency through Oct. 10, with trains departing every 30 minutes instead of the usual 15-minute intervals. The reduced schedule, which began Tuesday, allows crews from Denver Transit Partners to conduct repairs at the York-Josephine railroad crossing on a single track.

During the service reduction, trains will depart Denver's Union Station on the hour and half-hour, while trains leaving DIA will depart at 27 and 57 minutes past the hour. Regular A-Line service is scheduled to resume Oct. 11. Travelers heading to or from the airport are advised to plan additional time into their schedules and to consult RTD's service alerts page for updated route information.

The timing of the repair work coincides with a major storm system forecast to bring significant rainfall to the Denver metro area midweek, which could increase demand for public transit options. RTD has not indicated whether the weather event will affect the repair timeline.

stories.headline: RTD weighs future direction: serve more riders or cover a larger geographic area
stories.summary:
The Regional Transportation District is preparing to undertake a major analysis of its transit network, called RTD Connect, that will ask a fundamental question: Should the agency prioritize serving the largest number of riders, or providing coverage across the broadest geographic area? The Board of Directors was set to receive an in-depth briefing on the project Tuesday but canceled the work session so staff could develop more detailed examples of how each approach would affect the network before presenting to the board and at community workshops.

A ridership-focused system would offer faster and more frequent service along fewer routes, potentially reducing pollution and traffic while encouraging walkable development, according to project manager Doug Monroe. A coverage-based model would spread basic service as widely as possible to meet essential transit needs for those who depend on public transportation, even in areas with lower ridership.

The planning effort also comes as RTD staff considers cutting $20 million in routes and services starting in spring 2027 to address the agency's ongoing budget deficit. Board members have expressed concern about engaging communities in areas that currently have little RTD service but still pay into the regional transit tax.

Stakeholder workshops and public engagement sessions originally scheduled over the next six weeks have been pushed back with no replacement timeline announced. Director Michael Guzman called on board members to work together toward a clear direction despite the complexity of the decision.

stories.headline: K-9 deputy locates three missing children who wandered 1.5 miles from Buena Vista campsite
stories.summary:
Three children — two 6-year-olds and a 9-year-old — were found safe Saturday afternoon after wandering approximately 1.5 miles from their family's campsite near the Midland Bike Trail east of Buena Vista, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office. The children were part of a large family group from the Denver area. Family members searched for about two hours after noticing the children were missing around 9 a.m. before contacting law enforcement.

Chaffee County Search and Rescue responded with multiple drones, a helicopter and several foot teams. Sheriff's Office K-9 deputy Archie, known as 'Arch,' quickly picked up a scent at the campsite and led searchers in the direction the children had traveled. Search and rescue teams following the same path spotted the children from higher ground around 2 p.m. All three were uninjured.

Sheriff Andy Rohrich praised both the volunteer search and rescue teams and the K-9 unit for the swift resolution. 'We are so fortunate in Chaffee County to have such a highly trained and dedicated search and rescue team of volunteers for these terrifying moments,' Rohrich said in a social media post.

stories.headline: Six Colorado pro sports teams jointly endorse Ballot Issue 7A passenger rail expansion
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos, Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche, Colorado Rockies, Summit FC and Colorado Mammoth announced Tuesday a joint endorsement of Ballot Issue 7A, the November measure that would use a new sales tax to fund expanded daily passenger rail service along the Front Range. All six teams play near planned stations along the Colorado Connector route through the Denver metro area.

The endorsement brings together ownership groups that are otherwise rivals, including the Broncos' Walton-Penner Family Ownership Group and the Rams' Kroenke Sports and Entertainment — which owns the Nuggets, Avalanche and Mammoth — who faced off just two nights earlier in a Sunday Night Football game. Broncos president Damani Leech said the rail line would give fans across the state another convenient way to attend games, while KSE executive vice president Mike Neary noted Ball Arena's proximity to Union Station.

The Colorado Connector's planned route includes special event stops near the Broncos' proposed Burnham Yard stadium site and near Summit FC's planned Santa Fe Yards stadium district at Broadway and I-25. Rockies owner Dick Monfort and Summit owner Rob Cohen also offered endorsements, with Cohen saying the train would bring fans directly to the team's future home.

Ballot Issue 7A would impose a 0.333% sales tax on eligible purchases to expand the passenger rail system, which is already funded for three daily trips between Denver and Fort Collins beginning in 2029. If approved, the tax would fund additional trips and extend service south to Colorado Springs and Pueblo.

stories.headline: Rockies 2026 postmortem: Starting pitching woes drive fourth straight 100-loss season
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies finished the 2026 season with 104 losses, completing a fourth consecutive 100-loss campaign — the first team to accomplish that since the New York Mets from 1962 to 1965. The club's starting pitching was the primary culprit, posting baseball's worst rotation ERA for a fifth straight season at a combined 6.28, wiping out offensive improvements made since last year's franchise-worst 119-loss disaster.

Veteran additions Michael Lorenzen (7.08 ERA, released in August), Jose Quintana (11 starts before a season-ending elbow injury) and Tomoyuki Sugano all struggled or broke down. Returning starters fared no better: Kyle Freeland posted the second-highest ERA in baseball at 6.65 while Chase Dollander underwent season-ending elbow surgery in June. Rookie Tanner Gordon set a Rockies record with a 9.25 home ERA.

Manager Warren Schaeffer, entering the second year of a two-year deal in 2027, acknowledged the team must get creative with its pitching approach. 'We can't put a limit on how we're going to use (starting pitchers) next year,' Schaeffer said. New president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta and general manager Josh Byrnes face a challenging offseason further complicated by an expiring collective bargaining agreement.

One bright spot was Mason Adams, acquired from the White Sox in exchange for center fielder Brenton Doyle at the trade deadline. Adams made six starts and the organization is withholding final judgment on the centerpiece of that deal. DePodesta will need to find multiple pitching solutions before the 2027 season if the Rockies are to end their extended rebuild.

stories.headline: State health officials warn more than 400 Colorado stores sold contaminated marijuana vapes
stories.summary:
Colorado state health officials issued a warning that more than 400 retail stores across the state sold marijuana vaping products that were later found to be contaminated, raising public health concerns among consumers who purchased the affected items. Officials urged anyone who purchased vape products from the identified retailers to stop using them and to contact their healthcare provider if they are experiencing any adverse health effects.

The contamination warning follows a pattern of regulatory scrutiny on Colorado's cannabis vape market in recent months. Authorities have not specified the precise nature of the contaminants detected but indicated the affected products passed through licensed retail channels before the issue was identified.

State regulators are working to determine the source of the contamination and whether additional products may be affected. Consumers can check the state health department's website for a list of affected retailers and product batches. Officials said the investigation is ongoing.

topStory.headline: U.S. Forces Complete Withdrawal from Iraq, Ending Two-Decade Military Presence
topStory.summary:
The last American troops departed Iraq by Wednesday, September 30, formally closing a military presence that began with the 2003 invasion to topple Saddam Hussein and resumed in 2014 when U.S.-led coalition forces returned to help Iraqi forces defeat the Islamic State. The withdrawal was negotiated in 2024 under President Joe Biden and carried out by the Trump administration, which is simultaneously conducting military operations against Iran in the Arabian Sea under Operation Epic Fury. The departure marks the end of a engagement that cost 4,492 American lives during Operation Iraqi Freedom and another 123 during the subsequent campaign against ISIS, known as Operation Inherent Resolve.

Iran and its allied militia factions immediately claimed the withdrawal as a strategic victory. Abu Mojtaba al-Yasiri, a commander in the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed factions, called it "a historic victory for the Iraqi Islamic resistance groups and a crushing defeat for the American project." Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had told U.S. lawmakers in July that America remains Baghdad's "most important strategic partner" and that after September 30 Iraq's federal forces would be capable of protecting the country without armed factions.

Iraqi security analysts and Sunni community leaders have raised concerns that the departure is premature and could leave a dangerous power vacuum. Jasim al-Bahadli, an Iraqi security analyst who specializes in Shia armed groups, said the withdrawal removes a military counterweight to Tehran's influence and predicted that pro-Iranian militias would seek to convert the momentum into greater control over security and political decision-making. Abdulrahman al-Zobaie, a Sunni tribal leader in Fallujah, said that while all Iraqis aspire to full sovereignty, "the coalition leaving in this way and creating a vacuum is what all Iraqis fear."

The broader strategic consequences are significant. Iran-backed political movements and armed groups have steadily expanded their influence in Iraq since the 2003 removal of Saddam Hussein, whose government had fought Iran in a brutal eight-year war. The collapse of Iraqi security forces before ISIS in 2014 created a further opening for Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces, which became central to the fight against the extremists and have since embedded themselves in Iraqi political and military structures. Security experts warn the withdrawal could also allow the Islamic State, now reduced largely to sleeper cells, an opportunity to reconstitute amid reduced oversight.

The Iraq withdrawal, coming five years after the similarly abrupt U.S. exit from Afghanistan in 2021, closes both of the so-called post-September 11 "forever wars." Iraqi civilian deaths from direct violence during the 2003–2011 occupation are conservatively estimated between 180,000 and 210,000, with hundreds of thousands more believed to have died indirectly from the collapse of healthcare and infrastructure. The full geopolitical impact of the withdrawal will be shaped in part by the ongoing U.S. military campaign against Iran, two carrier strike groups currently operating in the Arabian Sea as the last American forces leave Iraqi soil.
